analysis.one_liner: Bans city and state governments from offering broadband or cable where a private company already does.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2005 with a single cosponsor and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal communications law to bar any state or local government — or an entity affiliated with one — from offering telecommunications, internet, or cable service in any area where a private company is already offering a substantially similar service [S2][S3]. It grandfathers government-run services that already existed when the bill became law [S2][S3]. In practice, this would shut down a city's ability to build its own broadband network wherever a private provider — even a minimal one — is present, and it also strikes a related provision from the cable-licensing law [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Incumbent cable and telephone companies would gain a federal shield against competition from city-built broadband networks: their mere presence in an area, offering any substantially similar service, would be enough to block a public alternative [S2][S3]. Residents of cities that wanted to build their own networks would lose that option [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit any state or local government or its affiliates from providing telecommunications, information, or cable service in any area where an unaffiliated private company offers a substantially similar service [S2][S3].
Would preserve the position of incumbent private providers by making their existing service a legal bar to a public alternative [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Residents and local governments would bear the cost: communities where private providers offer slow, expensive, or minimal service would lose the option of a publicly built alternative, and city-owned utilities that wanted to add broadband would be barred from new service areas [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban hinges on a private provider merely 'offering a substantially similar service,' so a company providing minimal or overpriced service could block a city from building a faster or cheaper public network [S2][S3].

Even supporters of private competition would have to acknowledge the bill overrides local decisions: a city that wanted to invest its own money in its own network would be barred by federal law from doing so [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows almost entirely to incumbent broadband and cable companies, which would gain federal protection from public competition. Its cost falls on residents and cities, particularly where private service is weak. There is no meaningful consumer-side provision in the bill text.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from the day it was introduced: referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its telecommunications subcommittee, and no hearing or vote ever happened before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill on May 26, 2005, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S1][S5].
On June 17, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where it remained with no further action for the rest of the 109th Congress [S5].
The bill never advanced beyond the subcommittee referral and received no floor vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Residents and city governments are better off than they would have been under the bill: the federal option of a publicly built broadband network was never taken off the table. Incumbent providers did not get the statutory shield they sought, though they lost nothing they had.

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit municipal governments from offering telecom or cable services where private companies do.

for.name: Rep. (sole cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the bill drew no other cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled after referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no recorded party split exists [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would make a private provider's existing service a federal legal bar to any city-built alternative, protecting incumbent revenue from public competition. Its interest runs against residents who want a faster or cheaper option [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Municipal utilities and government broadband networks
industries.note: Cities and their utilities would be barred from offering new telecom, internet, or cable service wherever a private company operates, ending a tool communities use when private service is inadequate. Only pre-existing government services would be grandfathered [S2][S3].
